newsitem.title: USA: Refiner plays keep U.S. sour crude market volatile.
newsitem.headline: Refiner plays keep U.S. sour crude market volatile.

text.p: U.S. cash crude prices firmed in Tuesday afternoon trade on strength in the gasoline market.
Traders in the Gulf said grade business featured a volatile sour crude sector, with stronger deals giving way to weaker bids as the session progresses.
At 1438 EDT (1838 GMT), September West Texas Intermediate/Cushing stood 5 cents higher at $19.80-90 a barrel, and the September/October roll was -4 cents.
West Texas Sour/Midland jumped higher in the early going to deals at $1.25 under the September benchmark, but has since moved back to talk around $1.40-1.30 under WTI/Cushing.
"There was early refiner buying, but that has since fallen away. It seemed like ratable barrel buying propped sour," said a cash dealer.
Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James last moved at a 25 cents premium, after selling earlier in the day at 23 cents over.
Midland/WTI barrels fetched deals at 29 and 30 cents below WTI, steady from Monday and in the rangebound stance the grade seems to levitate ad nauseam.
Factors at play for outright crudes continued to include Iraq, and when that country would return to selling oil under the U.N. "oil-for-food" accord.

A U.N. spokesman said earlier Tuesday that Secretary-General Kofi Annan and the secretariat would likely complete the review of Baghdad's aid distribution plan by week's end. Hundreds of pages of "annexes" must be reviewed before Annan offers approval.
Still, some crude traders think the process for getting Iraq back to market could be later than the mid-August date bantered about at the U.N.
"There is just as much of a chance Saddam (Iraq President Saddam Hussein) decides to delay this longer than there is for a quick restart in August," said a trader in Texas.
Iraq last week floated a different interpretation of when the oil sales clock should start, causing concern to many who see the move as the beginning of a new delaying tactic.

The U.N. Security Council said the clock started on June 8, the date the body approved an extension of the oil accord. Iraq, however, says the resolution governing the deal allows for the 180-day clock to start once the aid plan is in place.
The U.N. reading of the accord calls for Iraq to sell up to $1 billion of the $2 billion allowed during the first 90 days of the accord, by September 5.

Other than Iraq, traders said tonight's American Petroleum Institute (API) stock data should provide the lead for price direction. Estimates compiled by Reuters show expectations for a 2 million barrel draw in crude, a 1.75 million barrel build in distillates and a 1.70 million barrel gasoline draw.
